claim: AI stories run one plot line with no subplots 79% of the time versus 57% for human stories.

verdict.trueWording: far fewer subplots (79% 'no subplots' vs. 57%)
verdict.note: No quote supplied. §4.1 'Human authors subvert linearity' states the 79%/57% split exactly, and characterizes AI as favoring 'single-track narratives with fewer loose ends'.

claim: AI stories reach for smell imagery in 82% of stories versus 57% of human stories.

verdict.note: Exact figures in §4.1, same sentence family as the embodied-emotion finding.

claim: AI stories resolve through the protagonist's own action 69% of the time versus 46% for humans, and end ambiguously less often.

verdict.trueWording: more protagonist-driven resolutions (69% vs. 46%); humans comfortable with ambiguous endings
verdict.note: §4.1 matches both figures and states 'humans are more comfortable with ambiguous endings'; AI resolutions favor internal understanding/acceptance (47% vs 27%).

claim: Human protagonists' choices are framed as morally ambiguous in 59% of stories versus 38% of AI stories.
quote: frame protagonist' choices as more morally ambiguous

verdict.trueWording: frame protagonist' choices as more morally ambiguous
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim in the abstract (the paper prints a curly apostrophe in the same typo, 'protagonist’ choices'). §4.1 supplies the numbers as 'present morally ambivalent protagonists more often (59% vs. 38%)' — human 59%, AI 38%, as claimed.

claim: Human stories use chronological discontinuity, fourth-wall breaks (67% vs 39%), direct reader address (28% vs 7%) and named intertextual references (47% vs 24%) far more than AI stories.

verdict.trueWording: fourth wall (67% vs. 39%); reader directly (28% vs. 7%); specific texts (47% vs. 24%)
verdict.note: All three pairs appear exactly in §4.1 ('Human authors engage the outside world'), and 'Humans use more time jumps, flashbacks and flash-forwards, and nonlinear structure' covers chronological discontinuity. Note the three cited percentages are intertextuality/fourth-wall features, not temporal ones, despite the claim's 'temporal complexity' label.

claim: AI stories cluster in a shared region of narrative-feature space (human–AI centroid distance 1.6x AI–AI; 24.7% of human stories in the rarest decile vs 7.1% of AI).
quote: occupy a rarer, more dispersed region of narrative space

verdict.trueWording: occupy a rarer, more dispersed region of narrative space
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the Conclusion. §5 confirms both figures: 'mean human-AI centroid distance is 1.6× the mean AI-AI centroid distance (6.6 vs. 4.3)' and '24.7% of all human stories fall in the top 10% rarest stories corpus-wide, compared to just 7.1% of AI stories'.

claim: Narrative-level features still identify AI fiction at 93.9% macro-F1 after professional-style rewriting, so surface edits do not humanize structure.
quote: far harder to humanize

verdict.trueWording: far harder to "humanize"
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the Introduction (with 'humanize' in scare quotes). §4.2 confirms 93.9% macro-F1 on style-edited stories vs 95.5% unedited, a 1.6-point drop. One precision caveat: the rewriting is LAMP span-level artifact removal performed by Gemini itself using 25 few-shot examples from professional writers on 278 Gemini stories — not rewriting by professionals, so 'professional-style rewriting' is a loose gloss.

claim: Each model family has a signature: Claude's event intensity escalates less, GPT over-uses gossip and dream sequences, Gemini writes the tidiest endings.
quote: Claude produces notably flat event escalation

verdict.trueWording: Claude produces notably flat event escalation
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the abstract. All three fingerprints check out: §5 'Claude keeps it cool' ('event intensity escalates less than in any other source'); 'GPT likes to gossip' (gossip/rumor 64% vs 44-55%) plus the abstract's 'GPT over-indexes on dream sequences'; and 'Gemini produces the tidiest endings, extended denouements, and the bleakest settings'.

claim: LLM-processed text shows abrupt excess of style words such as delves (28x), showcasing (10x), intricate, underscores, pivotal, meticulously, realm; 2024 excess words were 66% verbs and 16% adjectives.
source: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát & Lause (arXiv 2406.07016; Science Advances 2025)

verdict.trueWording: delves (r=28.0), showcasing (r=10.2), underscores (r=10.9); 66% verbs, 16% adjectives
verdict.note: No quote supplied. Kobak et al. give delves r=28.0 and showcasing r=10.2 exactly, and 'hundreds of words have abruptly increased their frequency after ChatGPT became available'. The POS split is real but narrower than stated: 'Out of all 319 excess style words in 2024, 66% were verbs and 16% were adjectives' — style words, not all excess words. 'intricate' is the paper's own example of a style word; 'pivotal', 'realm' and 'meticulously' appear in the paper only as words identified by cited work (Liang et al. 2024b; Gray 2024) and in illustrative AI-style sentences, not in Kobak's own headline excess list.

feature: lexical overuse not inherited from training data

source: Juzek & Ward, Why Does ChatGPT Delve So Much? (arXiv 2412.11385, Dec 2024)
quote: Lexical overrepresentation remains a feature of current iterations of ChatGPT

verdict.trueWording: lexical overrepresentation remains a feature of current iterations of ChatGPT
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in §7 (sentence-internal, so lowercase 'lexical'). Appendix A's table of 21 focal words contains every word named in the claim: delve/delves/delved/delving, showcasing, underscores, intricate, garnered, boasts, groundbreaking, realm, aligns. §4 and Appendix B confirm the words are not overrepresented in pre-LLM corpora (arXiv, LCC, PubMed, Wikipedia). claim: Readers become wary of signature words like delve and may judge a text on those words rather than its content.
quote: wary of the word 'delve'

verdict.trueWording: wary of the word "delve"
verdict.note: Verbatim in the Introduction ('participants became wary of the word "delve" in the first sentence of an abstract') and echoed in §6 as 'Wariness about the word "delve"'. Caveat on the second half: the paper's line about judging on words rather than content is a speculation about rushed, underpaid RLHF evaluators — 'Rushed human evaluators might base their evaluations on the presence of particular words rather than on content' — not a finding about readers generally.

quote: linguistically more complex and verbose yet less creative

verdict.trueWording: LLMs generate stylistically complex stories, but tend to fall short

The core proposition — more complex yet less creative — is supported: the abstract says LLMs 'generate stylistically complex stories, but tend to fall short in terms of novelty, surprise and diversity,' and lists linguistic complexity among the measured dimensions. The specific verbosity evidence (unique words, dependency path length, noun and adjective counts) is absent; searches for 'verbos', 'unique words', 'dependency', 'noun', 'adjective' returned zero hits.

claim: Writers given GPT-4 story ideas produced stories 10.7% more similar to one another and 5.2% more similar to the AI prompts, while individual ratings rose mostly for low-creativity writers.
quote: collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced

verdict.trueWording: collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced
verdict.note: Quote matches word for word, and the page is confirmed as Doshi & Hauser (Science Advances, GPT-4 ideas). Concentration of individual gains among low-creativity writers is supported ('especially among less creative writers'). IMPORTANT CORRECTION: 10.7% is misdescribed. The paper says the similarity increase 'represents 10.7% and 8.9% of the total range' of similarity scores (an 8.10-point range) — not that stories were 10.7% more similar to one another. Separately, 5.2% more similar to the AI ideas is the ONE-idea condition; the five-idea condition is 5.0%. A different 10.7% elsewhere on the page refers to novelty gains for low-DAT writers, which may be the source of the conflation.

claim: People cannot detect AI-written self-presentations and rely on cues (first person, contractions, family topics) that AI can exploit to seem more human than humans.
quote: intuitive but flawed heuristics

verdict.trueWording: intuitive but flawed heuristics
verdict.note: Quote matches word for word, and authorship (Jakesch, Hancock, Naaman) is confirmed on the page. Every element of the claim is supported by the abstract: participants (N=4,600) 'were unable to detect self-presentations generated by state-of-the-art AI'; the named cues are 'first-person pronouns, use of contractions, or family topics'; and exploitability is stated as producing text perceived as 'more human than human.'

claim: Burrows' Delta on most-frequent words shows LLM stories clustering tightly by model while human stories spread widely; newer GPT-4 is tighter than GPT-3.5.

verdict.trueWording: display a higher degree of stylistic uniformity, clustering tightly by model

claim: 11,800 gpt-4o-mini stories for 236 nationalities conform to a single small-town, return-to-tradition, community-event plot with conflict sanitised and tension downplayed.
quote: Real-world conflicts are sanitised, romance is almost absent

verdict.trueWording: Real-world conflicts are sanitised, romance is almost absent

verdict.trueWording: prioritises stability above change and tradition above growth

claim: Professional authors' CREATIVITY INDEX (share of text not reconstructible from web n-grams) is 66.2% higher than LLMs', and RLHF alignment lowers LLMs' index by 30.1%.
source: Lu, Sclar, Hallinan, Mireshghallah et al., AI as Humanity's Salieri (arXiv 2410.04265)
quote: on average 66.2% higher than that of LLMs

verdict.trueWording: "is on average 66.2% higher than that of LLMs"
verdict.note: Abstract: CREATIVITY INDEX of professional human authors 'is on average 66.2% higher than that of LLMs, and that alignment reduces the CREATIVITY INDEX of LLMs by an average of 30.1%.' Both figures exact. Two small glosses, neither material: the abstract says 'alignment' where the claim says 'RLHF alignment', and the claim's parenthetical definition ('share of text not reconstructible from web n-grams') paraphrases the paper's construction of the index by reconstructing a text from web snippets via DJ SEARCH.

claim: Instruction-tuned models use present participial clauses 2–5x the human rate (GPT-4o 5.3x, d=1.38), e.g. 'Bryan, leaning on his agility, dances around the ring'.

verdict.trueWording: "present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the rate"
verdict.note: The quote field is empty, but the example sentence quoted inside the claim appears word for word: 'Bryan, leaning on his agility, dances around the ring, evading Show's heavy blows.' All figures exact: 'the instruction-tuned LLMs used present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the rate of human text' and 'GPT-4o uses present participial clauses at 5.3 times the rate of humans (paired Cohen's d = 1.38)'.

claim: Instruction-tuned LLMs use nominalizations 1.5–2x, 'that' subject clauses 2.6x and phrasal coordination 1.9x human rates, producing a noun-heavy academic style regardless of genre.
quote: informationally dense, noun-heavy style

verdict.trueWording: "informationally dense, noun-heavy style"
verdict.note: Quote appears verbatim twice. Figures confirmed: nominalizations 'at 1.5 to 2 times the rate of humans' generally, and for GPT-4o specifically ''that' clauses as subject 2.6 times as often (d=0.77), nominalizations 2.1 times as often (d=1.23), and phrasal coordination 1.9 times as often (d=0.81)'. Two glosses: the 2.6x and 1.9x figures are GPT-4o-specific, not all instruction-tuned models; and 'academic' is the claim's word, not the paper's, though the paper does attribute the style to instruction tuning across a diverse array of genres.

claim: GPT-4o uses camaraderie 162x, tapestry 155x, intricate 119x, underscore 107x, amidst 100x human rates; GPT-4o-mini palpable 145x; words that connote complex relations produce hollow summative sentences.

The 'complex relations' rationale is verbatim too: 'many of these words connote some form of complex relation among objects (e.g., tapestry, intricate, camaraderie, cacophony, amidst)... may signal a preference for grandiose, if hollow, summative sentences.'

claim: LLMs fail to vary style by genre or context the way humans do, so fiction-appropriate words become conspicuous elsewhere and the same style is applied everywhere.

verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the discussion ('...in ways similar to humans'). The conspicuousness half is also directly supported: 'words that are unremarkable in fiction are highly conspicuous and unconventional when used other genres,' plus the finding that LLMs 'struggle to match the stylistic variation present in human communication.'

Similarly phrases such as weight of, sense of, mix of occur very rarely or not at all in original seed paragraphs... while they occur frequently in LLM-generated responses.' One imprecision: the paper reserves 'syntactic templates' for its part-of-speech n-gram analysis (Table 8) and files these three phrases under recurrent awkward words/phrases; the claim merges the two.

source: Xu, Jojic, Rao, Brockett & Dolan, Echoes in AI (PNAS 2025-09-02; arXiv 2501.00273)

verdict.trueWording: "plot elements that are echoed across a number of generations"
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the abstract. Counts exact: 'in 50 out of 100 generations, the policeman gives instructions to take the second left... In 16/100 of the generations, a bakery is mentioned as a landmark.' Cross-model and tail claims both supported: elements 'echoed frequently across generations and across different LLMs,' while human-written stories 'contain plot elements that land far in the tail -- or not at all -- of LLMs' output distribution.'

claim: LLM stories show 7–9x higher 'drop ratios' than human stories, meaning a suspenseful element is resolved immediately after it peaks instead of being developed.
source: Xu et al., Echoes in AI (PNAS 2025)

verdict.trueWording: "LLM-generated stories lead to 7–9 higher drop ratio than human-written ones"
verdict.note: No quote supplied. Figure confirmed in Section 5 (the page literally reads '7–9 higher drop ratio', the multiplication sign apparently lost in the HTML build). Mechanism supported: 'a high drop ratio indicates that the Sui Generis score decreases immediately after the peak at position i, without progressively unraveling the surprising plot,' associated with 'abrupt resolutions that leave key suspenseful plot elements unresolved.' Slight tension in the claim's gloss: the paper's drop measures a surprising element being dropped or hastily closed off, sometimes left unresolved, rather than strictly 'resolved'.

claim: GPT-4 stories are Man-in-a-Hole over half the time and Rags-to-Riches 13.0% (humans 4.4%), while Riches-to-Rags (1.3% vs 14.6%) and Oedipus (1.7% vs 9.3%) arcs nearly vanish.

verdict.note: Quote verbatim. claim: Major Setback and Climax arrive about 10–15% earlier in GPT-4 narratives, and human stories sustain higher suspense with the gap widening from midpoint to end.
quote: higher levels of suspense

verdict.trueWording: "a substantial advancement (i.e., early occurrence) of TP4 and TP5"
verdict.note: The quote 'higher levels of suspense' IS verbatim ('human-written stories consistently exhibit higher levels of suspense'), as is the widening gap ('the gap begins to enlarge as the plot progresses from the midpoint (0.5 relative position) towards the end'). Downgraded from VERBATIM because the claim's magnitude is unsourced: the strings '10%' and '15%' appear nowhere in the paper, and the earlier arrival of Major Setback (TP4) and Climax (TP5) is reported only qualitatively plus a violin plot (Figure 2) with no numeric positions. The '10–15% earlier' figure appears to be eyeballed from that figure.

claim: By the 100-Endings metric, professional New Yorker fiction stays unpredictable near the close (no-rate 0.607) while top LLM stories collapse to 0.215, retaining only 23% of tension peaks versus 52%.

verdict.trueWording: "On EQ-Bench, LLMs (81–84) comfortably outscore all human datasets (44–78)"
verdict.note: No quote supplied. claim: LLM story character networks are denser (0.338–0.470 vs 0.182), more positive (mean edge weight 0.236–0.659 vs −0.061) and more clustered than human science-fiction, with far less variability.
quote: less conflict-driven social dynamics

verdict.trueWording: less conflict-driven social dynamics
verdict.note: arXiv 2510.18932v1, Nonaka & Perry. Quote verbatim. Table 1 in the raw HTML confirms density 0.338–0.470 vs human 0.182, clustering 0.623–0.766 vs 0.485, human mean edge weight −0.061 ('the only negative average edge weight'). ONE CORRECTION: the LLM edge-weight range is 0.235–0.659 (GPT-4o Mini = 0.235), not 0.236–0.659. Human corpus is confirmed science fiction (Project Gutenberg, genre-filtered, n=168).
